hints: Count carbon environments separately for the side chain and the ring, remembering that symmetry makes the two ortho carbons equivalent and the two meta carbons equivalent.
walkthrough:
Separate ring from side chain**
Look at $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. The two side chain carbons are in completely different environments, the $\text{CH}_2$ carbon and the $\text{C=O}$ carboxyl carbon, so that is 2 peaks already.

Use symmetry of monosubstituted benzene**
The benzene ring is monosubstituted, so it has a plane of symmetry through the substituent. That gives 4 ring environments: ipso (C attached to $\text{CH}_2$), 2 equivalent ortho, 2 equivalent meta, and para. So $4 + 2 = 6$ different carbon environments in total.
Final answer: number of peaks = 6

hints: Order the three by how easily they lose $\text{H}^+$ by thinking about carboxylic acid vs phenol vs alcohol typical strength.
Recall what stabilises the carboxylate anion in phenylethanoic acid, focusing on the electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ group.
Compare the O lone pair in phenol, which can interact with the ring, with the O lone pair in ethanol, which is localised and pushed by an alkyl group.
Link each structural feature to weakening or strengthening of the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilisation or destabilisation of the anion formed.
walkthrough:
Think acidity as anion stability**
Acidity is about how easily $\text{HA} \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$. The more stable the anion $\text{A}^-$ formed, the further this equilibrium lies to the right and the stronger the acid. So always compare the anions.

Why carboxylic acid wins**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, the $\text{C=O}$ group is strongly electron withdrawing by the negative inductive effect. It pulls electron density away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond, weakening it, and it disperses the negative charge on the carboxylate anion, stabilising it. That makes phenylethanoic acid the most acidic.

Why phenol is in the middle**
In phenol, the lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the benzene pi system. This overlap pulls electron density away from O, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond, and the resulting phenoxide anion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge into the ring. It is less effective than the carboxylate stabilisation, so phenol is weaker than the acid but stronger than an alcohol.

Why ethanol is weakest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, there is no delocalisation and no withdrawing group. The ethyl group is electron donating by the positive inductive effect, pushing electron density onto O. This strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and concentrates negative charge on the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ anion, destabilising it. So ethanol hardly releases $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: phenylethanoic acid (most acidic) > phenol > ethanol (least acidic)
Phenylethanoic acid is strongest due to negative inductive electron withdrawing effect of C=O which weakens O-H bond / stabilises the carboxylate anion.
Phenol is stronger than ethanol because the oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring which weakens O-H bond / stabilises the phenoxide anion.
Ethanol is weakest because the electron donating ethyl group strengthens O-H bond / destabilises the ethoxide anion.

hints: Remember $\text{AlCl}_3$ acts as a Lewis acid accepting $\text{Cl}^-$ from $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ to leave $\text{CH}_3^+$.
walkthrough:
See AlCl3 as a chloride acceptor**
$\text{AlCl}_3$ is electron deficient. It takes $\text{Cl}^-$ from chloromethane. Write the balanced ionic equation: $$\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$$ The methyl carbocation is the electrophile for the next step.

hints: Start the first curly arrow from inside the benzene hexagon to the $\text{CH}_3^+$ electrophile to show the pi electrons attacking.
Draw the Wheland intermediate with one $sp^3$ carbon bearing H and $\text{CH}_3$, a positive charge delocalised in the ring, and a broken ring of delocalisation.
Finish by showing the $\text{C-H}$ bond breaking to reform the aromatic ring, with the arrow going back into the ring and $\text{H}^+$ expelled.
walkthrough:
Electrophilic attack by benzene**
Benzene is electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting from inside the hexagon, representing the pi electrons, pointing to the $\text{CH}_3^+$ carbon. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond.

Draw the intermediate correctly**
The carbon attacked becomes $sp^3$, bonded to H and to $\text{CH}_3$. Aromaticity is temporarily lost. Show the intermediate as a cyclohexadienyl cation with a + charge and only two double bonds remaining in the ring. This is the Wheland or arenium ion.

Restore aromaticity**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on that same tetrahedral carbon back into the ring. The bond breaks, the pi system reforms, and $\text{H}^+$ leaves. The product is methylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$. The $\text{H}^+$ later reacts with $\text{AlCl}_4^-$ to regenerate $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system (inside hexagon) to $\text{CH}_3^+$; arenium intermediate with $\text{CH}_3$ and H on one tetrahedral carbon and + charge in ring; curly arrow from C-H bond into ring to reform aromatic $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ + $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Recognise that bromination of the methyl side chain, not the ring, needs homolytic cleavage of $\text{Br}_2$, so think of the condition that generates $\text{Br}$ radicals.
walkthrough:
Spot side chain vs ring**
The product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, so Br has replaced a benzylic H on the side chain, not added to the ring. That is free radical substitution. You need $\text{Br}_2$ with UV light to form $\text{Br}$ radicals by homolysis. No $\text{FeBr}_3$ or $\text{AlBr}_3$ carrier, which would give ring bromination.
Final answer: $\text{Br}_2$ + UV light

hints: Work backwards from phenylethanoic acid: hydrolysis of which functional group gives $\text{-COOH}$, and what precursor comes from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ by substitution of Br?
walkthrough:
Extend by one carbon via nitrile**
Step 3 converts Q into $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. The classic route to a carboxylic acid with one extra carbon is acid hydrolysis of a nitrile. So Q must be the nitrile $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, formed by $\text{CN}^-$ displacing $\text{Br}^-$ from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Final answer: Q is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ (phenylacetonitrile)

hints: For step 2, recall the nucleophile that replaces Br by CN and the alcoholic solvent and heating needed for this substitution.
For step 3, recall how to hydrolyse a nitrile fully to a carboxylic acid using aqueous acid and strong heating.
walkthrough:
Conditions for nitrile formation**
Step 2 is nucleophilic substitution: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$. Use KCN (or NaCN) in ethanol with heat. Ethanol is used because the organic bromide is not soluble in water and you want substitution, not hydrolysis to an alcohol.

Conditions for hydrolysis to acid**
Step 3 is hydrolysis: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$. Use dilute HCl(aq) with heat under reflux or boiling. Strong heating is needed because nitrile hydrolysis is slow.

Final answer: step 2: KCN in ethanol, heat
step 3: HCl(aq), heat / reflux / boil

hints: Think what happens if the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ product still has benzylic H atoms that can be attacked again by $\text{Br}$ radicals.
walkthrough:
See further radical substitution**
Free radical bromination does not stop cleanly after one Br. The product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ still has benzylic hydrogens, so further attack gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHBr}_2$ and then $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CBr}_3$. Any viable organic by-product such as these is accepted.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHBr}_2$ or $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CBr}_3$
